fields.meta_title: Assessment Form Builder That Scores Each Answer | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an assessment form that rates each criterion, adds up the score, and alerts the right person when a result falls short. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build an Assessment Form That Totals the Score
fields.hero_description: Build an assessment form that scores each answer, totals the result, and saves every assessment to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Working Assessment Form Needs
fields.features_subheading: A blank sheet records ratings. These parts turn the ratings into a score someone can act on.
fields.feature_1:
Rating scales with points behind them

Set a scale for each criterion, such as 1 to 4, and write what every level means. Assessors tap a rating, and the form stores the label and the points side by side on the record.
fields.feature_2:
Weighted totals worked out on submit

Give each section a share of the total, say 40 of 100 points for security. The weighted score is calculated the moment the assessor submits, and nobody adds up columns afterward.
fields.feature_3:
Cut-offs that decide the next step

Choose the total that calls for action and name who acts on it. A low total can open a review, book a coaching session, or message a manager in Slack with the record attached.
fields.feature_4:
Notes and photos as evidence

Let assessors attach a photo or a short note to any rating. The evidence stays on that line of the record. A reviewer can see why a criterion got a 2 before signing off on the total.
fields.feature_5:
Every assessment in one database

Each submission becomes a row you can filter by assessor, date, or site. Compare this month with last, export the rows to a spreadsheet, or connect them to the other tools you use.
fields.feature_6:
Source code you can take with you

Export the full code of your assessment app to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A developer can host it on your own servers or wire it into the school or HR system you use.

fields.usecase_heading: Where Assessment Forms Do the Scoring
fields.tab_content_1:
Each rating counts, and Ava finishes with 13 of 16

Ms. Harlow grades ninth-grade science presentations against four criteria worth 4 points each. While Ava Lindqvist presents, Ms. Harlow rates research, clarity, visuals, and answers to questions on her tablet. The form adds the ratings to 13 of 16 and writes the score into Ava's row of the class gradebook.
fields.tab_content_2:
Likelihood and severity multiply into 16 for the blocked exit

The night supervisor at Tillman Logistics walks the warehouse with the hazard form on his phone. Each hazard gets a likelihood and a severity on a 1 to 5 scale, multiplied together. A blocked fire exit rated 4 and 4 scores 16, over the limit of 12. Dana Cole, the safety manager, gets a Slack message with the photo.
fields.tab_content_3:
Brightline's weighted score of 64 sends it to IT

Procurement at Halvern Foods scores each new supplier out of 100: security is worth 40 points, delivery 35, and price 25. Brightline Packaging earns 22, 28, and 14, a total of 64. Any supplier under 70 goes to the IT lead for a security review before a contract is drafted, and Brightline now sits first in her queue.
fields.tab_content_4:
Day 30: four reps go live, one gets coaching

At day 30, the support trainer at Quayside rates five new hires on six skills, each on a 1 to 4 scale. Four reps clear every skill and start taking live tickets on Monday. Jordan Hale scores a 2 on refunds, and the form books a coaching session with his team lead, Erin Walsh.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Assessment Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create an assessment form that scores every criterion and flags results under your cut-off, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Weight the criteria and set the cut-off
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the decision the assessment feeds before drafting a question: a grade, a go-live date, a signed contract. That decision tells you which criteria matter and which score should send the result to someone for action.
fields.howto_step_2_des: List the criteria an assessor judges, usually four to eight. Each one should describe something observable, like "cites two sources" instead of "good research". Merge criteria that overlap, because an overlap scores the same strength or weakness twice.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose a scale, usually 1 to 4 or 1 to 5, and write one line for every level of every criterion. Two assessors reading that line should land on the same rating. Labels like "fair" and "good" are where their scores drift apart.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Give the criteria that matter most a larger share of the total. Then pick the score that triggers action and the person who acts. Try the cut-off on three past cases you already judged by hand and see whether it agrees.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste the criteria, level descriptions, weights, and cut-off into the prompt. Emergent builds the form and its scoring logic, along with the database behind it. Name who hears about a low score, and change any part later by prompting again.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Send results where they are used
fields.howto_step_6_des: Route each finished assessment to the place it is acted on, whether that is a gradebook, a Slack channel, or a supplier record. Email the person assessed a copy of their ratings when your process calls for it.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Fill the form as an assessor and give one criterion a deliberately low rating. Check the total, confirm the alert reaches the right person, and open the saved record. Then ask a second assessor to score the same case and compare the two.

plan.angle: The top 10 is blank paper: Jotform and Formplus templates, Canva and template.net designs, a Pinterest board, a hospital's patient assessment PDF, a ScienceDirect definition and a Welkin help article. Each one records ratings and stops there. An assessment exists to reach a judgment, and on paper someone still adds the columns, compares the total with a cut-off and tells the person who acts. This page treats the form as the scorer: points behind every rating, weights per section, a threshold that routes the result, and every assessment saved as a row. It covers four settings that score differently (a classroom rubric, a hazard walk, a weighted supplier score, a 30-day skills check) and stays off performance reviews, interviews and fitness testing, which have their own pages.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build an Assessment Form That Totals the Score', meta title 'Assessment Form Builder That Scores Each Answer | Emergent' and hero 'Build an assessment form that scores each answer, totals the result, and saves every assessment to a database you own.' (117 chars) state the whole job; how-to description is one sentence under 140 chars.

intent.evidence: Top 10 is templates and a definition; FAQ 1 defines the term, FAQ 4-5 cover types and template fields, FAQ 8-10 cover employee, student and patient versions, and the 7-step how-to builds one.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: 'Set a scale for each criterion, such as 1 to 4, and write what every level means'; 'Try the cut-off on three past cases you already judged by hand'.

openers.evidence: Every paragraph and feature body opens on a full sentence: 'Ms. Harlow grades ninth-grade science presentations...', 'Give each section a share of the total...', 'Let assessors attach a photo...'.

craft.evidence: No tacked-on endings or run-on sentences; the 15 serial lists are a note (QC Q8 P2), not blocking.

voice.evidence: Plain operator voice: 'Labels like "fair" and "good" are where their scores drift apart.' No hype vocabulary.

truth.evidence: Numbers agree: 4+3+3+3=13 of 16; 4x4=16 over 12; 22+28+14=64 under 70; 4 of 5 reps go live. FAQ 3, 4, 10 match the Queen's, UNL, WTCS and UAB sources; Emergent claims map to prompt-build, database-owned, no-caps, alerts, code-export, free-start.

distinct.evidence: Four scoring settings (rubric, hazard multiply, weighted supplier, 30-day skills) are distinct from fitness-assessment-form and employee-evaluation-form; QC D2 clean.

faq.evidence: 10 items, answer-first, FAQ 1/3/4 verbatim AlsoAsked (verbatim check ok, PAA gate 10 pass 0 reject), hub link in item 2, sibling links in items 8 and 10, no brand or format in any question.

images.evidence: Contact sheet: each tab draws its copy's names and numbers (Ava 13 of 16; blocked fire exit 16, Dana Cole Slack; Brightline 64, IT lead queue; Jordan Hale refunds 2, Erin Walsh); table rows add up (Corliss 77, Dunmore 76, Ashby 86).
